name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Electron flow and polarity in Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents a Daniell cell operating spontaneously under standard conditions (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)):

Which of the following correctly describes the direction of electron flow, conventional current, and polarity of the zinc electrode?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a Daniell cell with a zinc electrode dipped in \(1\text{ M }\mathrm{ZnSO}_{4}(\mathrm{aq})\) and a copper electrode dipped in \(1\text{ M }\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}(\mathrm{aq})\), connected internally by a salt bridge and externally through a voltmeter. Standard cell potential is \(1.1\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a galvanic cell, the electrode where oxidation occurs is the anode and carries a negative potential with respect to the solution, while the electrode where reduction occurs is the cathode and carries a positive potential. Conventional current flows opposite to the direction of electron flow.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Anode (oxidation): \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\)
Cathode (reduction): \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)
Overall reaction: \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because zinc has a lower standard reduction potential (\(-0.76\text{ V}\)) than copper (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)), zinc atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions, leaving electrons on the zinc rod. Thus, the zinc electrode is negatively charged. These electrons travel through the external metallic wire from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode, where \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions accept them and deposit as copper metal. Consequently, conventional current flows from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The electron flow from anode to cathode and opposite current direction match standard galvanic cell behaviour. Therefore, electrons flow from zinc to copper, conventional current flows from copper to zinc, and the zinc electrode is negatively charged.

answer.text: Electrons flow from copper to zinc; current flows from zinc to copper; zinc electrode is positively charged.
Electrons flow from zinc to copper; current flows from copper to zinc; zinc electrode is negatively charged.
Electrons flow from zinc to copper; current flows from zinc to copper; zinc electrode is negatively charged.
Electrons flow from copper to zinc; current flows from copper to zinc; zinc electrode is positively charged.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Standard hydrogen electrode representation and potential

questiontext.text:
Observe the diagram of the reference half-cell shown below:

What is the standard cell notation and assigned standard electrode potential of this half-cell at \(298\text{ K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram depicts a platinum electrode coated with finely divided platinum black dipped in \(1.00\text{ M }\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\) solution, with pure \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) bubbled through at \(1\text{ bar}\) pressure.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
According to IUPAC convention, the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) serves as the universal reference electrode and is assigned a standard reduction potential of exactly zero at all temperatures.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The half-cell reaction is:
\[\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\]
In standard cell notation, phase boundaries are represented by a single vertical line (\(\mid\)), starting from the inert metal electrode, followed by the gas, and then the aqueous ion.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Combining the inert platinum conductor, hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ bar}\), and \(1\text{ M}\) hydrogen ions gives the notation \(\mathrm{Pt(s)} \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}}) \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}})\). Its assigned standard potential at \(298\text{ K}\) (and all temperatures) is \(0.00\text{ V}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The notation includes all three phases in proper sequence and assigns zero potential. Thus, the correct representation and potential are \(\mathrm{Pt(s)} \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}}) \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}})\) and \(E^{\ominus} = 0.00\text{ V}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Pt(s)} \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}}) \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}})\), \(E^{\ominus} = +0.34\text{ V}\)
\(\mathrm{Pt(s)} \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}}) \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}})\), \(E^{\ominus} = -0.76\text{ V}\)
\(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}}) \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}}) \mid \mathrm{Pt(s)}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +1.10\text{ V}\)
\(\mathrm{Pt(s)} \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1\text{ bar}}) \mid \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq, 1\text{ M}})\), \(E^{\ominus} = 0.00\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Daniell cell under opposing potential exceeding 1.1 V

questiontext.text:
The circuit diagram shows a Daniell cell connected to an external variable DC source \(E_{\text{ext}}\) opposing the cell potential (\(1.1\text{ V}\)) such that \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\):

Which of the following correctly identifies the electrode processes occurring under this condition?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A Daniell cell with standard emf \(1.1\text{ V}\) is opposed by an external voltage \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), with electrons shown flowing from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
When \(E_{\text{ext}}\) exceeds \(1.1\text{ V}\), the cell no longer acts as a galvanic cell; it functions as an electrolytic cell in which electrical energy drives the non-spontaneous reverse reaction. Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation occurs at the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Electrons enter the zinc electrode, so reduction takes place at zinc (cathode):
\[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}\]
Electrons leave the copper electrode, so oxidation takes place at copper (anode):
\[\mathrm{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since electrons flow from copper to zinc, copper metal is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions (dissolving at the copper anode), while \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions in the zinc sulphate solution gain electrons and deposit as metallic zinc at the zinc cathode. Conventional current flows from zinc to copper.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Reversing the spontaneous Daniell cell reaction requires external energy (\(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\)), resulting in copper dissolving at the anode and zinc depositing at the cathode.

answer.text: Copper dissolves at the copper anode and zinc is deposited at the zinc cathode.
Zinc dissolves at the zinc anode and copper is deposited at the copper cathode.
Both copper and zinc dissolve simultaneously without any metal deposition.
No chemical reaction takes place and current in the circuit drops to zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Wheatstone bridge measurement of solution resistance

questiontext.text:
The Wheatstone bridge arrangement shown below is used to determine the unknown resistance \(R_{2}\) of a conductivity cell containing an ionic solution:

When no current passes through the detector P, what is the resistance \(R_{2}\) of the conductivity cell, and why is an alternating current (AC) oscillator O used instead of a DC source?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the Wheatstone bridge circuit: \(R_{1} = 120\text{ }\Omega\), \(R_{3} = 200\text{ }\Omega\), and \(R_{4} = 500\text{ }\Omega\) at the null (balanced) point when no current flows through detector P.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At balance, the potential difference across detector P is zero, and the ratio of resistances in adjacent arms is equal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a balanced Wheatstone bridge as configured in the diagram:
\[R_{2} = \frac{R_{1} R_{4}}{R_{3}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given resistances into the balance equation:
\[R_{2} = \frac{120\text{ }\Omega \times 500\text{ }\Omega}{200\text{ }\Omega} = \frac{60000}{200}\text{ }\Omega = 300\text{ }\Omega\]
An AC source (oscillator O in the audio frequency range) is used instead of DC because passing direct current through an ionic solution causes electrochemical reactions that change the composition of the solution.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the bridge ratios: \(\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}} = \frac{300}{120} = 2.5\) and \(\frac{R_{4}}{R_{3}} = \frac{500}{200} = 2.5\), confirming balance. Therefore, \(R_{2} = 300\text{ }\Omega\), and the AC source prevents change in composition of the solution.

answer.text: \(48\text{ }\Omega\); AC source increases the degree of dissociation of the electrolyte.
\(833.3\text{ }\Omega\); AC source eliminates the cell constant of the conductivity cell.
\(300\text{ }\Omega\); AC source prevents change in composition of the ionic solution.
\(300\text{ }\Omega\); AC source converts ionic conductance into metallic conductance.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Molar conductivity variation for strong and weak electrolytes

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the variation of molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\)) with \(c^{1/2}\) for aqueous solutions of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\):

Which statement accurately explains the steep rise in \(\Lambda_{m}\) for \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) at low concentrations compared to the gradual linear increase for \(\mathrm{KCl}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m}\) against \(c^{1/2}\) for \(\mathrm{KCl}\) (a strong electrolyte) and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) (a weak electrolyte). The \(\mathrm{KCl}\) line rises slowly and linearly as \(c^{1/2} \rightarrow 0\), while the \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) curve rises very steeply near \(c^{1/2} \rightarrow 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Molar conductivity is given by \(\Lambda_{m} = \kappa V\), where \(V\) is the volume of solution containing \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrolyte.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For strong electrolytes: \(\Lambda_{m} = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\).
For weak electrolytes: degree of dissociation \(\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}\) increases with dilution according to Ostwald's dilution relation.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Strong electrolytes like \(\mathrm{KCl}\) are already completely dissociated at all concentrations, so dilution merely reduces interionic attractions, giving a slow linear rise. In contrast, weak electrolytes like \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) have a low degree of dissociation at higher concentrations. Upon dilution, especially in dilute solutions, the degree of dissociation increases sharply, substantially increasing the total number of ions in the volume containing \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrolyte and causing \(\Lambda_{m}\) to shoot up steeply.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The steep upward curve for acetic acid is thus caused by the sharp increase in degree of dissociation upon dilution.

answer.text: The limiting molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) can be obtained directly by linear extrapolation to \(c^{1/2} = 0\).
The degree of dissociation of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) increases sharply on dilution, increasing the number of ions per mole of electrolyte.
The conductivity (\(\kappa\)) of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) increases rapidly with dilution while that of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) decreases.
Acetic acid is completely ionised at all concentrations, whereas \(\mathrm{KCl}\) is only partially ionised.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Cathode reaction and complex formation in dry cell

questiontext.text:
The cross-sectional diagram of a commercial dry cell (Leclanché cell) is shown below:

During the discharge of this cell, what is the change in oxidation state of manganese at the cathode and the coordination complex formed by \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a dry cell consisting of a zinc cup acting as the anode, a central carbon (graphite) rod acting as the cathode, and a moist paste of \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\), carbon black, \(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}\), and \(\mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}\) between the electrodes.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a primary dry cell, oxidation occurs at the zinc anode and reduction occurs at the carbon cathode surrounded by \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Anode reaction: \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\)
Cathode reaction: \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2} + \mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO(OH)} + \mathrm{NH}_{3}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\), let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) be \(x\): \(x + 2(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4\).
In \(\mathrm{MnO(OH)}\), let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) be \(y\): \(y + (-2) + (-1) = 0 \Rightarrow y = +3\).
Thus, manganese is reduced from the \(+4\) oxidation state to the \(+3\) oxidation state. The ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\)) liberated at the cathode combines with \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions to form the tetraamminezinc(II) complex ion, \([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both the oxidation state change (\(+4 \rightarrow +3\)) and the complex formula (\([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}\)) are consistent with the dry cell chemistry. Therefore, manganese is reduced from \(+4\) to \(+3\) and forms \([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}\).

answer.text: Manganese is reduced from \(+4\) to \(+3\) oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) forms \([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}\).
Manganese is reduced from \(+7\) to \(+4\) oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) forms \([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{2}]^{2+}\).
Manganese is oxidised from \(+2\) to \(+4\) oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) forms \([\mathrm{ZnCl}_{4}]^{2-}\).
Manganese is reduced from \(+4\) to \(+2\) oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) forms \([\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q07 - Electrode reactions in hydrogen oxygen fuel cell

questiontext.text:
The schematic below shows a \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell using porous carbon electrodes impregnated with catalysts and concentrated aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) electrolyte:

Which pair of half-cell reactions correctly represents the processes at the anode and cathode?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The fuel cell uses \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) fed at the anode, \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) fed at the cathode, and concentrated aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) as the alkaline electrolyte, producing \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) as the overall product.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the electrolyte is strongly alkaline (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)), \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\) ions participate directly in both electrode half-reactions rather than \(\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\) ions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Overall reaction: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).
Oxidation of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) occurs at the anode, and reduction of \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) occurs at the cathode.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At the anode, hydrogen gas reacts with hydroxide ions to form water and release electrons:
\[2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\]
At the cathode, oxygen gas reacts with water and electrons to regenerate hydroxide ions:
\[\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\]
Adding both half-reactions cancels \(4\mathrm{e}^{-}\), \(4\mathrm{OH}^{-}\), and \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\), yielding \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both half-reactions are balanced for mass and charge and sum to the net combustion reaction of hydrogen. Therefore, the anode reaction is \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\) and the cathode reaction is \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\).

answer.text: Anode: \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\); Cathode: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\)

Anode: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\); Cathode: \(4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\)

Anode: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\); Cathode: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\)

Anode: \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\); Cathode: \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Determining constant A and molar conductivity from KCl plot

questiontext.text:
The linear plot of \(\Lambda_{m}\) versus \(c^{1/2}\) for dilute aqueous \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solutions at \(298\text{ K}\) is shown below, with y-intercept \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} = 150.0\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and a plotted point at \((0.020, 148.25)\):

Using the graph, calculate the constant \(A\) in \(\Lambda_{m} = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\) and the molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m}\) of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) at \(c = 0.0009\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the linear graph, the y-intercept at \(c^{1/2} = 0\) is \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} = 150.0\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), and another point on the line is \((c^{1/2}, \Lambda_{m}) = (0.020\text{ (mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}, 148.25\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1})\). Target concentration \(c = 0.0009\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(\mathrm{KCl}\) is a strong 1–1 electrolyte obeying the Debye–Hückel–Onsager linear relation at low concentrations, with slope equal to \(-A\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Lambda_{m} = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\]
\[A = -\text{slope} = \frac{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{m}}{c^{1/2}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, determine \(A\) using the two points \((0, 150.00)\) and \((0.020, 148.25)\):
\[A = \frac{150.00 - 148.25}{0.020 - 0} = \frac{1.75}{0.020} = 87.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\]
Next, compute \(c^{1/2}\) for \(c = 0.0009\text{ mol L}^{-1}\):
\[c^{1/2} = \sqrt{9 \times 10^{-4}} = 3 \times 10^{-2} = 0.030\text{ (mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\]
Now substitute into the equation for \(\Lambda_{m}\):
\[\Lambda_{m} = 150.00 - 87.5 \times 0.030 = 150.00 - 2.625 = 147.375 \approx 147.38\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(0.030 > 0.020\), \(\Lambda_{m}\) at \(0.0009\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) must be slightly less than \(148.25\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), which \(147.38\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) satisfies. Thus, \(A = 87.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\) and \(\Lambda_{m} = 147.38\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q09 - Molar conductivity from conductivity cell dimensions

questiontext.text:
A cylindrical conductivity cell of uniform cross-sectional area \(A = 0.785\text{ cm}^{2}\) and electrode separation \(l = 50\text{ cm}\) is filled with \(0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ NaOH}\) solution, as shown below. Its measured electrical resistance is \(5.55 \times 10^{3}\text{ }\Omega\):

What is the molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\)) of this \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of solution column \(l = 50\text{ cm}\), cross-sectional area \(A = 0.785\text{ cm}^{2}\), resistance \(R = 5.55 \times 10^{3}\text{ }\Omega\), and molarity \(c = 0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The solution is uniform between the two parallel platinised platinum electrodes, so resistance follows \(R = \rho\frac{l}{A}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resistivity: \(\rho = \frac{RA}{l}\)
Conductivity: \(\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho} = \frac{l}{RA}\)
Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, calculate the resistivity \(\rho\):
\[\rho = \frac{5.55 \times 10^{3}\text{ }\Omega \times 0.785\text{ cm}^{2}}{50\text{ cm}} = \frac{4356.75}{50} = 87.135\text{ }\Omega\text{ cm}\]
Next, calculate the conductivity \(\kappa\):
\[\kappa = \frac{1}{87.135\text{ }\Omega\text{ cm}} = 0.011476\text{ S cm}^{-1} \approx 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\]
Finally, calculate the molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m}\):
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^{3}\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = 229.6\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \(\frac{\text{S cm}^{-1} \times \text{cm}^{3}\text{ L}^{-1}}{\text{mol L}^{-1}} = \text{S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\). The magnitude is consistent with a \(0.05\text{ M}\) strong base solution. Thus, \(\Lambda_{m} = 229.6\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_DIAGRAM_Q10 - Standard cell potential and Gibbs energy in iron corrosion

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the electrochemical corrosion of iron in the presence of moisture and air, with the anodic and cathodic half-cell standard potentials indicated:

For the overall corrosion cell reaction \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\), calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\) (take \(F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the corrosion diagram:
Standard reduction potential of the anodic couple: \(E^{\ominus}_{(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe})} = -0.44\text{ V}\)
Standard reduction potential of the cathodic couple: \(E^{\ominus}_{(\mathrm{H}^{+}|\mathrm{O}_{2}|\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})} = +1.23\text{ V}\)
Overall reaction: \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\), and \(F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the balanced overall equation, \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Fe}\) are oxidised to \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\), transferring \(n = 4\text{ mol}\) of electrons.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{anode}}\]
\[\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\):
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.23\text{ V} - (-0.44\text{ V}) = 1.67\text{ V}\]
Next, calculate \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\) with \(n = 4\):
\[\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -4 \times 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 1.67\text{ V} = -644620\text{ J mol}^{-1} = -644.62\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} > 0\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} < 0\), the corrosion reaction is strongly spontaneous under standard conditions. Therefore, \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -644.62\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

answer.text: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\), \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -644.62\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\), \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -322.31\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.79\text{ V}\), \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -304.94\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\), \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = +644.62\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
